points.title: Nominalisation et effacement du "je" en français formel
points.explanationEn:
Formal written French — administrative letters, business correspondence, academic essays, official reports — systematically prefers abstract nouns over verbs and impersonal or passive constructions over a visible first-person subject. This is not a stylistic accident; it is a structural expectation that a fluent reader of formal French unconsciously checks for, and its absence is what makes a native French reader instantly peg a piece of writing as translated-from-English, casual, or unpolished, even when every individual sentence is grammatically correct.

Nominalization means converting a verb (or an adjective) into its corresponding abstract noun and restructuring the sentence around that noun. Instead of writing 'nous avons décidé d'augmenter les prix parce que les coûts ont augmenté' (a chain of verbs, which reads as direct and almost conversational), formal register favors 'la décision d'augmenter les prix résulte de la hausse des coûts' (decision, increase — nouns doing the structural work, with the verbs reduced to a single linking résulte de). Common nominalizing suffixes to build actively: -tion/-sion (décider → décision, augmenter → augmentation, réduire → réduction), -ment (développer → développement, changer → changement), -ance/-ence (résister → résistance, exister → existence), and -age (bloquer → blocage). Once you have the noun, formal French likes to chain it into a longer, single sentence using de, par, and relative constructions rather than restarting with a new subject and verb — this is why formal writing tends to produce noticeably longer sentences than spoken French, which prefers short independent clauses linked loosely by et, donc, alors.

The second and related habit is avoiding je as the grammatical subject wherever the content allows it, replacing it with impersonal or passive alternatives. Instead of 'je vous informe que votre demande a été acceptée,' formal correspondence often prefers 'il est porté à votre connaissance que votre demande a été acceptée' or simply the passive 'votre demande a été acceptée,' letting the outcome — not the writer — occupy the subject position. Common impersonal frames include il convient de + infinitive (it is fitting to / one should), il importe de (it matters to), il y a lieu de (there is reason to), and il apparaît que (it appears that) — all of which push the human agent out of subject position and replace it with an impersonal il that carries no real referent. The passive voice (être + past participle) serves the same depersonalizing function for actions: la décision a été prise (the decision was made) rather than 'j'ai décidé' or even 'nous avons décidé.' On (used impersonally, roughly 'one') is generally AVOIDED in the most formal registers because it can read as vague or even slightly familiar — the passive or il + impersonal verb is preferred when the goal is maximal formality, even though on is grammatically available and used in more neutral registers.

The effect of combining nominalization with depersonalization is a register where the writer's presence recedes and the content — decisions, facts, procedures — appears to state itself. This is why a formal résignation letter says 'la présente lettre a pour objet de vous informer de ma décision de démissionner de mon poste' rather than 'je veux vous dire que je démissionne': the second sounds perfectly correct but reads as blunt and under-formal for the genre, precisely because it keeps je as the active subject of a plain verb instead of routing the content through the abstract noun décision and the impersonal frame la présente lettre a pour objet de.

examples.fr: La présente lettre a pour objet de vous informer de ma décision de quitter mes fonctions.
examples.en: This letter is to inform you of my decision to leave my position.
examples.note: nominalized décision instead of 'je décide de partir'; impersonal frame 'la présente lettre a pour objet'

examples.fr: Il convient de souligner que cette hausse résulte directement de l'augmentation des coûts de production.
examples.en: It should be noted that this increase results directly from the rise in production costs.
examples.note: impersonal il convient de + two nominalizations, hausse and augmentation, doing the work of two verbs

examples.fr: Votre candidature a été examinée avec la plus grande attention.
examples.en: Your application was examined with the utmost care.
examples.note: passive construction removes any named agent (who examined it is left unstated, as is standard in formal replies)

examples.fr: Il est porté à votre connaissance que le délai de traitement a été prolongé.
examples.en: Please be advised that the processing period has been extended.
examples.note: fully impersonal frame avoids both je and vous as grammatical subjects of the main verb

examples.fr: La mise en œuvre de cette réforme nécessitera une adaptation progressive des services concernés.
examples.en: The implementation of this reform will require a gradual adaptation of the departments concerned.
examples.note: mise en œuvre and adaptation are both nominalizations standing in for 'mettre en œuvre' and 's'adapter'

examples.fr: Il y a lieu de reconsidérer les modalités du contrat avant sa reconduction.
examples.en: There is reason to reconsider the terms of the contract before its renewal.
examples.note: il y a lieu de is a standard formal-register impersonal opener

examples.fr: Une réponse favorable serait grandement appréciée.
examples.en: A favorable response would be greatly appreciated.
examples.note: passive-adjacent construction (serait appréciée) avoids 'j'apprécierais'

examples.fr: L'annulation de la réunion s'explique par l'indisponibilité de plusieurs intervenants.
examples.en: The cancellation of the meeting is due to the unavailability of several participants.
examples.note: annulation and indisponibilité are nominalized forms of annuler and (ne pas être) disponible

examples.fr: Il apparaît que les objectifs fixés n'ont pas été atteints dans les délais impartis.
examples.en: It appears that the set objectives were not achieved within the allotted time.
examples.note: il apparaît que displaces a personal judgment ('je pense que...') into an impersonal observation

examples.fr: Le non-respect de ces conditions entraînera la résiliation immédiate du contrat.
examples.en: Failure to comply with these conditions will result in immediate termination of the contract.
examples.note: non-respect and résiliation are nominalizations that let the sentence avoid naming who fails to comply or who terminates

commonMistakes: Writing formal letters as chains of je + verb ('je vous informe... je vous demande... j'espère...'), which is grammatically fine but reads as under-formal for the genre compared to native models.
Overusing on as a default impersonal subject in high-formality documents, where native writers reach for the passive or il + impersonal verb instead.

Building nominalizations incorrectly by guessing the suffix, e.g. saying 'la décidation' instead of la décision, or 'l'augmention' instead of l'augmentation — these noun forms must be learned per verb, not generated by a single reliable rule.

Using the passive with an explicit par-agent when the whole point of formal register is to omit the agent, producing awkward hybrids like 'la décision a été prise par moi' instead of simply j'ai décidé or the fully impersonal la décision a été prise.

Overusing nominalization until the sentence becomes an unreadable stack of abstract nouns with no verb at all — formal register still needs a small number of strong linking verbs (résulter de, s'expliquer par, entraîner, nécessiter) to connect the nouns.
whyItTrips: English formal register leans on passive voice too, but far less on nominalization — English keeps more verbs where French would convert them to nouns, so a literal translation from English formal writing under-nominalizes and reads as too direct in French.

English speakers are taught that avoiding 'I' in formal writing is about politeness or hedging; French depersonalization is instead a structural register marker independent of politeness, which makes it easy to under-apply it in genuinely formal contexts (contracts, official letters) where it's obligatory rather than optional.

There's no productive, exceptionless rule for which nominalizing suffix a given verb takes (-tion vs. -ment vs. -age vs. -ance), so English speakers who are used to English's more regular -tion/-ing system default to guessing and produce non-words.

points.title: Subordination complexe et subjonctif après formules figées
points.explanationEn:
Beyond word choice, formal written French is distinguished by SENTENCE ARCHITECTURE: where spoken and casual written French favor short, loosely linked independent clauses, formal register favors single, longer sentences built from a main clause with one or more subordinate clauses nested inside it, often stacked two or three deep. Mastering this means knowing the connectors that formal French uses to subordinate rather than coordinate, and knowing which of those connectors demand the subjunctive mood in the clause they introduce — a demand that is often invisible from the English translation, since the equivalent English connector doesn't touch the verb form at all.

A large family of formal set phrases that open or structure a subordinate clause require the subjunctive as a matter of fixed grammar, regardless of whether the content expresses doubt, emotion, or certainty — the mood is triggered by the phrase itself, not by the speaker's attitude. Afin que and pour que (so that, expressing purpose) always take the subjunctive: 'nous vous transmettons ce dossier afin que vous puissiez l'examiner' (so that you may examine it) — puissiez, not pouvez, even though there's no doubt the recipient is being asked to examine it. À moins que (unless), avant que (before), and jusqu'à ce que (until) behave the same way: 'veuillez confirmer votre présence avant que la réunion ne débute' uses ne débute (subjunctive) not débute. Note also the ne explétif — that extra, meaning-empty ne that appears in very formal register after avant que, à moins que, craindre que, and a few others; it adds no negation and is a pure register marker, correct to include in high-formality writing and correct to omit in neutral writing, but never analyzed as a real negative.

A second family of formal connectors introduces a subordinate clause of consequence or concession and takes the indicative or subjunctive depending on the specific connector — this is where English speakers most often guess wrong, because English 'so that' can mean either purpose (subjunctive-triggering afin que) or result (indicative-taking de sorte que/si bien que), and the two are grammatically distinct in French. De sorte que and si bien que, when they express a REALIZED result ('it worked out such that...'), take the indicative: 'il a reformulé sa demande, de sorte que le dossier a été accepté' (he reworded his request, so that/such that the file was accepted — a fact, indicative). But de sorte que can also express intended purpose, in which case it switches to the subjunctive — the same connector, two different moods, depending purely on whether the outcome is being asserted as fact or framed as a goal.

Finally, formal register nests subordinate clauses using relative pronouns beyond the basic qui/que — namely lequel/laquelle/lesquels/lesquelles (and their contracted forms auquel, duquel) after prepositions, and dont for de + noun — to avoid restarting sentences with demonstrative pronouns the way spoken French does. 'Le contrat, dont les termes ont été renégociés, entrera en vigueur le premier janvier' packs a whole additional clause about the contract's terms into a single sentence using dont, where spoken French would more likely say 'le contrat — on a renégocié ses termes — il entrera en vigueur...' as two separate ideas. Similarly, ce dont, ce à quoi, and moyennant quoi let formal writing refer back to an entire preceding idea (not just a noun) inside a single continuing sentence, a level of syntactic compression that is one of the clearest markers of accomplished formal French.

examples.fr: Nous vous prions de bien vouloir nous faire parvenir les documents requis afin que votre dossier puisse être traité dans les meilleurs délais.
examples.en: We kindly ask you to send us the required documents so that your file can be processed as soon as possible.
examples.note: afin que + puisse (subjunctive), fixed by the connector itself, not by any doubt about the outcome

examples.fr: Veuillez confirmer votre présence avant que la réunion ne débute.
examples.en: Please confirm your attendance before the meeting begins.
examples.note: avant que triggers the subjunctive (débute) and the formal ne explétif, which carries no negative meaning

examples.fr: Il a reformulé sa demande de sorte que le dossier a finalement été accepté.
examples.en: He reworded his request, such that the file was ultimately accepted.
examples.note: indicative (a été accepté) because de sorte que here reports a realized result, not a goal

examples.fr: Nous avons révisé le calendrier de sorte que chaque équipe puisse respecter les délais impartis.
examples.en: We revised the schedule so that each team can meet the assigned deadlines.
examples.note: subjunctive (puisse) because de sorte que here expresses purpose, not an accomplished fact — same connector, opposite mood from the previous example

examples.fr: Le contrat, dont les termes ont été intégralement renégociés, entrera en vigueur le premier janvier.
examples.en: The contract, the terms of which have been fully renegotiated, will come into effect on January first.
examples.note: dont compresses 'les termes du contrat' into a single relative clause nested inside the main sentence

examples.fr: Les mesures auxquelles vous faites référence n'ont pas encore été validées par le comité.
examples.en: The measures you are referring to have not yet been validated by the committee.
examples.note: auxquelles, the contracted form of à + lesquelles, required because faire référence à takes the preposition à

examples.fr: À moins que le conseil ne s'y oppose formellement, la proposition sera adoptée dès la semaine prochaine.
examples.en: Unless the board formally objects to it, the proposal will be adopted as early as next week.
examples.note: à moins que + subjunctive (s'oppose) with the optional formal ne explétif

examples.fr: Le comité poursuivra ses délibérations jusqu'à ce qu'un consensus soit trouvé.
examples.en: The committee will continue its deliberations until a consensus is reached.
examples.note: jusqu'à ce que always takes the subjunctive (soit), regardless of how likely the consensus is

examples.fr: Ce à quoi nous nous engageons, c'est à garantir la transparence de l'ensemble du processus.
examples.en: What we are committing to is guaranteeing the transparency of the entire process.
examples.note: ce à quoi refers back to the whole idea of s'engager à, a compression spoken French would avoid

examples.fr: Moyennant quoi, l'administration se réserve le droit de suspendre la procédure.
examples.en: In consideration of which, the administration reserves the right to suspend the procedure.
examples.note: moyennant quoi, a formal connector referring to an entire preceding clause, has no natural single-word English equivalent

commonMistakes: Using the indicative after purpose connectors like afin que and pour que because the English 'so that' doesn't mark mood, producing afin que vous pouvez instead of the required afin que vous puissiez.

Confusing de sorte que / si bien que as always taking one mood, when in fact the mood depends entirely on whether the clause reports a realized result (indicative) or an intended purpose (subjunctive) — the same French connector, different moods, based on meaning alone.

Dropping dont and defaulting to que + a possessive workaround (e.g., 'le contrat que ses termes ont été renégociés' instead of le contrat dont les termes ont été renégociés), because English 'whose'/'of which' doesn't map onto a single relative pronoun the way dont does.

Misreading the ne explétif after avant que, à moins que, or craindre que as a real negation and mistranslating the sentence's meaning (thinking 'avant qu'il ne parte' means 'before he doesn't leave' rather than simply 'before he leaves').

Chaining short independent clauses with et/donc/alors in formal writing instead of subordinating them with afin que, dont, lequel, or de sorte que, which produces grammatically correct but noticeably under-formal prose for the genre.
whyItTrips: English 'so that' collapses two grammatically distinct French ideas (purpose, always subjunctive with afin/pour que, versus result, indicative with de sorte que/si bien que in factual use) into one phrase, so English speakers have no native intuition telling them these should ever differ.

English relative pronouns (which, whose, that) don't inflect for gender, number, or preceding preposition, so the French system of qui/que/dont/lequel/auquel/duquel — each tied to a specific grammatical role — has to be learned as a structural system rather than mapped word-for-word.

The ne explétif looks exactly like a negation to anyone pattern-matching on ne, so English speakers who've been taught 'ne...pas = not' assume any bare ne before a verb must be negating something, when in formal register it is often purely decorative.
